For these, 10% applies only up to the value of the rest of the work, and the part above that goes at 22%.

In the price list you mark which items are beni significativi (significant goods). When the job is maintenance on a home and you buy the materials, the draft asks you, for each marked line, how much the good is worth within that line: the price also includes fitting, and only you know the value of the good. With that figure, the IVA comes out split between 10% and 22%, and the PDF states it. If the customer buys the goods themselves, or if it's a renovation, the split isn't needed. The guide on [IVA on home work](/guide/iva-preventivo-lavori-casa) explains how it works in detail.

The calculation follows your answers and the rules of the Agenzia delle Entrate (the Italian tax authority), but it isn't tax advice: every quote carries a notice to check with your accountant (commercialista).

sezioni.titolo: How we treat your prices
paragrafi: **They stay yours.** Price list, quotes and business details are yours, and on request we send you the price list in Excel and the PDFs of your quotes. We don't sell the data and we don't use it for advertising.

**They only serve your own quotes.** The price list is tied to your business: your drafts only search among your items, and your items never go into anyone else's quotes. To choose the items the system looks at names and descriptions; it takes the price afterwards, from your price list.

**No invented figures.** A price in the draft comes from one of your items, or you type it yourself. If you upload the price list from a PDF or photos, the file is only used to read the items and is not kept afterwards.
When you stop using PreventivoLampo, your data is deleted within the times set out in the privacy notice, except what the law requires us to keep.

voci.d: How many items do I need to get started?
voci.r: There's no minimum: start with the jobs you do most often. Anything missing stays to be priced, and with the tick 'suggest adding it' the price list fills out as you work.

voci.d: I have different prices for private customers and for businesses. What do I do?
voci.r: There's one price list. In the draft you can change the price of a line for that quote, and the price list stays as it is.

voci.d: If I put a price up, do quotes I've already sent change?
voci.r: No. A quote already prepared keeps the prices it was created with, and an approved one never changes. The new price applies from later drafts.

voci.d: My price list is a handwritten notebook. Is that OK?
voci.r: Yes. Take photos of the pages, more than one at a time if you like, and upload them. The system transcribes the items and marks where it isn't sure, and you check every price before importing.

voci.d: Can I correct an item after importing it?
voci.r: Yes. In the price list you open the item and change the name, price, unit and the words you use for it out loud, and you mark whether it's a bene significativo (significant good) or whether the price includes the material. After an import these two ticks are empty: it's worth checking them on the items you use most.

voci.d: What is the tick 'the price includes the material' for?
voci.r: It tells the system that the item is supply and fit. If you say the customer is buying the material, the line doesn't take that price: it becomes labour only and stays to be priced, unless the draft finds one of your labour-only items.

meta.titolo: How to write a quote for home work
meta.descrizione: How to write a quote for home work: details, items with quantities and units, IVA, timings, payments, exclusions and variations. Plus the mistakes that cost the most.

come-fare-un-preventivo.riga: What to write, line by line, so the quote holds up even after the customer has signed it.
come-fare-un-preventivo.h1: How to write a quote for home work that holds up until the final payment
come-fare-un-preventivo.intro: A quote isn't only there to say how much a job costs. When the customer accepts it, it becomes the contract: it's the sheet you'll pull out if halfway through the job they ask for an extra socket, if they pay late, or if at the end they say the skirting board was included. This guide lays out what has to be in it, in the order you'd write it, with the rules of the codice civile (civil code) and the codice del consumo (consumer code) that really matter in home work. It works for an electrician as much as for a building firm, and it applies even if you write the quote by hand.
inBreve: When the customer accepts, the quote is the contract: write it as if you had to read it out in front of a judge.
Every item has a quantity, a unit and a price, and says what it includes: supply, fitting, disposal.
Always write what's excluded, how many days the offer is valid for, and how the deposit and the final payment are made.
Variations must be authorised in writing: the codice civile (civil code) expressly requires it.
If the customer is a private individual and signs at home, they normally have 14 days to change their mind, and you have to tell them.

sezioni.titolo: An accepted quote is a contract
paragrafi: Under the codice civile (the Italian civil code), a contract is concluded when the person who made the offer learns that the other side has accepted it (art. 1326). Your quote is the offer. The customer's signature, or their online acceptance, closes the contract. From that moment, what you wrote binds you, and what you didn't write will be decided by someone else.

In most home jobs that contract is an **appalto** (a works contract): the person doing the work organises the means needed and works at their own risk, for a fee in money (art. 1655). If you work alone or nearly alone, with your own personal labour and no real organisation of employees, the relationship can instead be a **contratto d'opera** (a contract for personal work, art. 2222). The difference isn't just theory: for example, the warranty periods change, as you'll see below.

If the quote has no price, the codice civile says it is worked out from the standard rates or customary prices and, failing that, the judge sets it (art. 1657). A quote that says «price to be agreed» doesn't protect you: it hands you over to an expert appointed by the court.

sezioni.titolo: Who you are, who the customer is, where the work is
paragrafi: The first part looks like paperwork, but it's what makes the document usable. Put your company name, partita IVA (VAT number), address, phone number and email. For the customer you need their first name and surname (or company name), their home address and the site address, if it's different. If you'll have to invoice later, you'll need their codice fiscale (tax code) too: asking for it straight away saves a phone call later.

When the customer is a consumer and the contract is made at their home or at a distance, the codice del consumo (the Italian consumer code) asks for exactly these things: your identity, address, phone number and email, before they commit (art. 49). It's not a formality: the burden of proving you gave them is on you.

Then one line about the job: where (floor, room, outside), what you're doing and what the starting point is. «Bathroom on the second floor, complete refit, existing sanitaryware and tiles to be removed» already says half the quote and fixes the starting condition, which you'll need if you find a surprise under the tiles.

sezioni.titolo: The items: quantity, unit and what's included
paragrafi: The heart of the quote is the lines. Each line has four things: a description the customer understands, a quantity, a unit of measure and a unit price. The line total is the product, and the customer should be able to redo it with the calculator on their phone.

The most common units in home jobs are the square metre (walls, floors, plasterboard), the linear metre (skirting boards, chases, pipework), the piece (light points, sanitaryware, windows and doors), the hour (fault finding, small jobs) and the «corpo» (a lump sum, one single price for a whole item). Choose the unit you really measure with, not the one that makes the number look smaller.

punti.titolo: Supply and fit, or fit only
punti.testo: Write whether the line includes the material. «Supply and fit of 80x120 shower tray» and «Fitting of shower tray supplied by the customer» are two different prices, and mixing them up is the most common dispute at the end of a job.

If the price depends on quality, name the product or at least the range. A «standard» socket or tap means nothing to the customer, who at the end of the job will expect the ones they saw in the shop window.

Protecting floors and furniture, demolition, transport and disposal of waste materials, making good, final cleaning, scaffolding or mobile towers, the dichiarazione di conformità (declaration of conformity) for installations. If you do them, put them on a line; if you don't, put them in the exclusions.

If the customer hasn't decided how many sockets they want, don't make up a number. Leave the quantity open and tell them, or write a number with the phrase «indicative quantity, the actual number will be charged». It's the simplest way not to lose either money or trust.

sezioni.titolo: Prices, IVA and total
paragrafi: Under the lines put the taxable amount (imponibile), the IVA rate, the IVA amount and the total. To a private customer who makes the contract at home or at a distance, you must state the **total price including taxes**, or at least how to calculate it (art. 49 of the codice del consumo). A quote with only the net amount, sent to a private customer, is a recipe for hearing «I understood a different figure».

The customer doesn't choose the rate and neither do you: it depends on the type of property, the type of work and who buys the materials. In homes it's often 10%, with a separate calculation for the beni significativi ("significant goods", such as boilers, windows and doors, and sanitaryware). The guide on [IVA on quotes for home work](/guide/iva-preventivo-lavori-casa) explains the cases one by one. If you're in the regime forfettario (flat-rate tax scheme), on the other hand, you don't charge IVA to the customer on the invoice, and it's a good idea to write that in the quote too.

A system like PreventivoLampo asks you three things (whether it is a home, what kind of work it is, who buys the materials) and works out the rate from there, with the split of the beni significativi (significant goods, a rule of Italian VAT) on the items you have marked in your price list. At the moment it calculates 10%, 22% and that split; inversione contabile (reverse charge), 4% first home and the flat-rate regime not yet, so in those cases check the total before sending it. The final word is yours and your accountant's.

sezioni.titolo: Timing, validity of the offer and payments
paragrafi: Write when you can start and how long the job lasts, in working days or weeks, and what can move the date: delivery of a material chosen by the customer, the weather for outside work, a permission the customer has to ask for. A date with no conditions becomes a promise; a date with its conditions is information.

Then the **validity of the offer**. If you write that the quote stays valid for a certain number of days, you're bound to keep it for that time: under the codice civile, if the person making the offer has committed to keeping it open, revoking it has no effect (art. 1329). It protects the customer, but it protects you too: once the deadline has passed, if material prices have changed, you can redo the sums.

On payments, choose your words with care. An **acconto** (a payment on account) is an advance on the price. A **caparra confirmatoria** (a confirmatory deposit) is something else: if the customer doesn't perform, you can withdraw and keep it; if you don't perform, they can ask you for double (art. 1385). Writing «caparra» when you mean «acconto» changes the consequences.

For long jobs it's best to be paid in stages (stati di avanzamento). The codice civile provides for this for works carried out in parts: you can ask for payment in proportion to the work done, and payment makes the customer presumed to have accepted the part paid for, while simple payments on account don't (art. 1666). Unless agreed otherwise, the balance is due when the customer accepts the finished work (art. 1665).

sezioni.titolo: Exclusions, variations and unforeseen problems
paragrafi: The exclusions section is the one that saves you the most time at the end of the job. Write clearly what you don't do: the chases are closed by the bricklayer, painting after the installation is not included, someone else fits the light fittings, the council paperwork is handled by the customer's surveyor. An exclusion line costs ten seconds; an argument about something taken for granted costs a day and often a customer.

Then variations. Under the codice civile you can't change how the work is done unless the customer has authorised it, and **the authorisation has to be proved in writing** (art. 1659). If the price was fixed as one single figure for the whole job, even authorised changes don't entitle you to extra pay, unless that was agreed. The customer, for their part, can ask you for changes as long as they don't exceed one sixth of the total price, and you're entitled to be paid for the extra work (art. 1661).

The practical way to handle all this is to put unit prices in the quote even when you give a lump-sum total, and to get every variation signed, even with a written message, before you do it. The guide on [lump sum or measured](/guide/preventivo-a-corpo-o-a-misura) goes into detail.

For real unforeseen problems, the ones nobody could have seen, the codice civile provides for a price revision if the cost of materials or labour changes by more than one tenth of the total price, for the part above that tenth only, and a fair payment for difficulties in carrying out the work caused by geological, water-related and similar conditions (art. 1664). These rules can be excluded by contract, so read carefully the quotes a bigger firm makes you sign.

sezioni.titolo: Acceptance, withdrawal and warranty
paragrafi: The quote must say how it is accepted: a dated signature under the sentence «I accept the quote and the conditions stated above», or an online acceptance that leaves a record of who, when and which version. With PreventivoLampo the customer accepts from the link, and the name, date, time and a copy of the accepted PDF are kept.

If the customer is a private individual and the contract is concluded at their home, or at a distance, the codice del consumo comes into play: as a rule they have 14 days to withdraw without giving a reason, and you must inform them and give them the form. If you don't, the period is extended by twelve months. It deserves a page of its own: [withdrawing from a quote accepted at home](/guide/recesso-preventivo-accettato-a-casa).

Finally the guarantee, which you don't write but which is worth knowing about. In an appalto (contract for works) the customer must report non-conformities and defects within sixty days of discovering them, and the claim lapses two years after delivery of the work (art. 1667 of the codice civile, the Italian Civil Code). In a contratto d'opera (contract for personal work) the periods are shorter: eight days from discovery to report, one year from delivery to take action (art. 2226). If the customer accepts the work and the defects were known or easy to spot, the guarantee is not due: that is why a signed end-of-works record is worth more than it seems. For serious defects in a building, though, you are liable for ten years (art. 1669), and the Corte di Cassazione (Italy's supreme court) applies this to renovations too. And if you also supply goods to a private customer, such as a boiler or a window, the guarantee of the codice del consumo (Consumer Code) applies to those goods.

sezioni.titolo: The mistakes that cost you money or customers
paragrafi: Almost every dispute over home jobs starts from a few lines badly written or never written. These are the mistakes that come up most often.

punti.testo: A single figure for ‘bathroom refit’ means you can't price a variation, and the customer can't see what they're paying for. Keep the breakdown even when the customer wants just one number.

If at the site visit you said ‘it'll be about thirty metres’, in the quote either write the measurement you actually took or write that the quantity will be worked out at the end of the job. A round number written with confidence turns into a fixed price.
The customer reads the quote as a list of things they will get. Anything that isn't excluded is, for them, included.

punti.titolo: Variations agreed by word of mouth
punti.testo: ‘While you're at it, move this socket too’ is how you lose the margin on a job. Write the variation down, price it and get it approved first.

punti.titolo: A quote that arrives a week later
punti.testo: People who ask for several quotes tend to go with whoever replies first and clearly. Writing it the same evening as the visit, when you remember every detail, is the simplest advantage you have. That is why the [quote by voice](/funzioni/preventivo-da-vocale) exists.
A quote with no expiry can come back to you six months later, accepted, at the material prices of back then.

voci.d: Is a quote signed by the customer a contract?
voci.r: Yes. The quote is an offer, and when the customer accepts it and you find out, the contract is concluded (art. 1326 of the codice civile, the Italian civil code). From then on the written terms apply to both of you.

voci.d: How long should a quote stay valid?
voci.r: You decide how long and you write it in the quote. If you commit to keeping the offer open for a set time, you can't withdraw it during that period (art. 1329 of the codice civile, the Italian civil code). For jobs with a lot of materials a short validity is best, because suppliers' prices change.

voci.d: Do I have to show the IVA in a quote to a private customer?
voci.r: Yes, it's always a good idea. If the contract is made at the customer's home or at a distance, the codice del consumo (Italian consumer code) requires you to state the total price including taxes, or how it is calculated (art. 49).

voci.d: Advance payment or caparra: which do I write?
voci.r: It depends on what you want. An advance payment (acconto) is a part payment of the price. A caparra confirmatoria (a deposit that confirms the contract) has specific effects if one side defaults: whoever received it can keep it, whoever paid it can ask for double back (art. 1385 of the codice civile, the Italian civil code). Use the right word, because the consequences are different.

voci.d: The customer asks for extra work during the job. How do I protect myself?
voci.r: Get the variation authorised in writing, with the price, before you do it: the codice civile (Italian civil code) requires written proof of the authorisation (art. 1659). If the quote has unit prices, working out the variation is quick.

voci.d: Can I ask to be paid in stages as the work progresses?
voci.r: Yes, if you put it in writing. For work carried out in parts, the codice civile (Italian civil code) lets you ask for payment in proportion to the work done (art. 1666). State in the quote the stages and the percentage or amount for each.

voci.d: How long am I liable for defects in my work?
voci.r: In an appalto (contract for works) the customer must report defects within sixty days of discovering them and can take action within two years of delivery (art. 1667 of the codice civile, the Italian Civil Code). If the relationship is a contratto d'opera (contract for personal work), the periods are eight days and one year (art. 2226). For serious defects in a building, though, you are liable for ten years (art. 1669), including in renovations. And if you also supply goods to a private customer, such as a boiler or a window, the guarantee of the codice del consumo (Consumer Code) applies to those goods.

meta.titolo: Fixed-price (a corpo) or measured (a misura) quote: the differences
meta.descrizione: Fixed-price (a corpo) or measured (a misura) quote: what the codice civile (Italian civil code) says, who carries the risk on quantities, how to handle variations and final measurements, with examples by trade.

preventivo-a-corpo-o-a-misura.riga: Fixed price or unit prices: who takes the risk on quantities and how to handle variations.
preventivo-a-corpo-o-a-misura.h1: Fixed-price (a corpo) or measured (a misura) quote: which to choose and how to write it
preventivo-a-corpo-o-a-misura.intro: ‘We'll do it a corpo’ (for a fixed price) and ‘we'll do it a misura’ (measured, at unit prices) are two phrases every tradesperson says and hears, often without the two sides meaning the same thing. Yet the choice decides who pays if the square metres come out higher than expected, how a variation is priced and how much arguing there is at the end of the job. This guide explains the difference in practice, what the codice civile (Italian civil code) says, when each formula suits you and how the final bill is settled, with examples for home trades.
inBreve: A corpo, there is a single price for the work described: the risk of having measured wrongly is yours.
A misura, the customer pays the unit prices on the quantities actually carried out: you only know the total at the end.
Even a corpo, it's worth writing the unit prices: you need them for variations and for work left out.
Variations must be authorised in writing, and a corpo they don't entitle you to extra pay unless you agreed it.

sezioni.titolo: The two formulas, in plain words
paragrafi: **A corpo** means the price covers the work as a whole, as described in the quote. ‘Painting the whole flat, walls and ceilings, two coats of emulsion’ at one price. If the walls then turn out a few metres bigger than planned, the price doesn't change.

**A misura** means the quote sets unit prices (per square metre, per metre, per item) and the total is worked out by multiplying them by the quantities actually carried out, measured at the end of the job or at progress stages. The quantities in the quote are an estimate; the real bill is the final one.

The codice civile (Italian civil code) doesn't use these two terms when it talks about appalto (contract for works), but it knows the situation well: it speaks of a price ‘determined globally’ for the whole work (arts. 1659 and 1661), which is the case of work a corpo. The sharper definitions come from public contracts, where case law describes the price a corpo as a fixed sum that doesn't change with quantities, and the price a misura as a price per unit that follows the actual quantity of work. In private jobs the language is the same, but what counts is what you write.

sezioni.titolo: Who takes the risk on quantities
paragrafi: The real difference between the two formulas is who pays for estimating mistakes. A corpo, the risk is yours: if you miscalculated the metres, or the wall to skim was in worse shape than it looked, the price stays the same. A misura, the risk is the customer's: if the quantities go up, the bill goes up, and they know that from the start.

The codice civile (Italian civil code) puts a limit on truly unforeseeable events. If, because of circumstances nobody could have foreseen, the cost of materials or labour rises or falls by more than a tenth of the total price, either side can ask for a revision, but only for the part above that tenth. And if during the work difficulties come up from geological, water-related and similar causes that were not foreseen and make the work much more costly, the contractor is entitled to fair compensation (art. 1664).

These rules also apply when the price is a corpo, unless the parties have clearly waived them. The Corte di Cassazione (Italy's highest court) has held that the rule can be derogated from and that an ‘a forfait’ (lump-sum) clause, by which the contractor also takes on the risk of unforeseen difficulties, is valid. If a client makes you sign a contract with a clause like that, know that you are giving up this protection.

sezioni.titolo: When it makes sense to work a corpo
paragrafi: A fixed price works when the job is well defined and you can measure all of it before you start. The customer likes it because they know straight away what they'll spend; it suits you because, if you work well, the margin you gain on organisation stays yours.

punti.titolo: Jobs you can see in full
punti.testo: Painting an empty flat, replacing six measured windows, fitting a kitchen: what needs doing is right in front of you and there are few surprises.
A private client comparing three quotes understands a fixed total better than a list of unit prices. A lump-sum price, with the breakdown underneath, is often the one that wins.

An honest lump-sum price includes a margin for risk. If you leave it out, you pay for any measuring mistake; if you set it too high, you lose the job. That's why a proper site visit and well-taken measurements are worth more than any discount.

sezioni.titolo: When it makes sense to work by measurement
paragrafi: Pricing by measurement is the right choice when you can't know the quantities beforehand. Asking for a fixed price in those cases means forcing you to inflate it or risk working at a loss.

punti.testo: How much plaster comes off, how much rubble goes out, what's under the old floor: you only know once you've opened it up. Price per square metre or per cubic metre, and measure the final quantities together.
Skim coats, plaster repairs, making good after chasing: you only find out how much surface needs fixing while you're working.

On jobs that last weeks, measuring by batches and being paid in proportion to the work done is also provided for by the codice civile (Italian Civil Code) for works carried out in batches (art. 1666).

sezioni.titolo: Variations: what the codice civile (Civil Code) says
paragrafi: Variations are where the two methods really part ways. The codice civile (Italian Civil Code) starts from a rule that always applies: you can't change how the work is done unless the client has authorised it, and **the authorisation has to be proved in writing** (art. 1659).

Then it adds a rule that concerns lump-sum work directly: even when the changes have been authorised, if the price of the whole job was set as a lump sum you have no right to extra payment for variations or additions, unless agreed otherwise (art. 1659). In plain words: if you work for a lump sum and the client asks for one more thing, the price of that extra thing must be written down and accepted, otherwise you risk doing it for free.

It's different when the client asks for changes within the limits of the law. The client can introduce variations as long as their amount doesn't exceed one sixth of the total agreed price, and you have the right to be paid for the extra work **even if the price was fixed as a lump sum** (art. 1661). This doesn't apply if the variations, even while staying under one sixth, significantly change the nature of the job or the quantities of the individual categories of work.

Finally, there are the variations needed to do the job properly. If you can't agree, the judge sets them together with the new price; if they exceed one sixth of the total price you can withdraw from the contract and obtain, depending on the circumstances, fair compensation, and if they are substantial the client can withdraw too, paying you fair compensation (art. 1660).

The practical result is just one: **even in a lump-sum quote, write the unit prices of the main items**. You need them to price in a minute the extra socket or the metre of skirting board less, and the client has already seen and accepted them.

sezioni.titolo: Final measurements: how to settle up without arguments
paragrafi: When you work by measurement, the delicate moment is the final measuring. It's best to decide in advance, and write down, how you measure: are surfaces measured as full wall area, or do you take out doors and windows? Is skirting board counted by metres of wall or by pieces fitted? Is tile waste included in the price per square metre? These are free choices, but they have to be made beforehand, because once the job is done everyone will remember the version that suits them.

Take the final measurements together with the client, or whoever represents them, and write them on a sheet signed by both. On long jobs the same goes for each stage. The codice civile (Italian Civil Code) says that, for works carried out in batches, either party can ask for each batch to be checked, and that payment makes the paid part presumed accepted; simple advance payments don't have this effect (art. 1666).

In the quote you can also use a mixed formula, which is very common: a lump-sum total for the part that is certain and measured prices for the part you can't predict, for example «demolizioni e ripristini a misura secondo i prezzi unitari indicati» (demolition and making good by measurement at the unit prices shown). It's often the fairest solution for both sides.

sezioni.titolo: Examples by trade
paragrafi: Habits change from one trade to another. These are the most common practices in home work, with the units you'll also find on the dedicated pages, for example the one on the [painter's quote](/preventivo-imbianchino) or the [bricklayer's quote](/preventivo-muratore).

punti.testo: Often a lump sum per room or per flat, with the square metre of walls and ceilings as a fallback unit price. Skim coats and anti-mould treatments are better priced by measurement, because you only see the surface to treat once the work has started.
Laying per square metre, skirting and trims per linear metre, special cuts and steps per piece. Write down whether waste is included and who supplies adhesive and grout.

The «a punto» (per point) way of working is in effect work by measurement: each light point or socket has its price and the total follows the number of points installed. The consumer unit and the dichiarazione di conformità (declaration of conformity) are often a lump sum.
A bathroom refit is often a lump sum, with a list of water points and waste outlets; long pipe runs and leak tracing by measurement or by the hour.

Demolition and removal per square or cubic metre, partition walls and plastering per square metre, chasing per metre: this is where pricing by measurement is most common. For a full renovation the client almost always asks for an overall price, and the mixed formula is the one that holds up best.
Walls and suspended ceilings per square metre, with openings and bulkheads counted separately. Windows and doors per piece, with sizes and model stated, and fitting as a lump sum for each opening.

domande.titolo: Questions about lump-sum and measured pricing

voci.d: In a lump-sum quote, do I still have to write the quantities?
voci.r: It's always a good idea. The quantities and unit prices under the total show the client what they're buying and let you quickly work out variations and work left out. You can write that the price is a lump sum and that the breakdown is only for variations.

voci.d: If the lump-sum job turns out to have more metres than expected, can I ask for more?
voci.r: As a rule, no: on lump-sum work the risk on quantities is yours. What remains are the protections in the codice civile (Italian Civil Code) for unforeseeable events, such as costs rising by more than a tenth of the price or unforeseen geological and water difficulties (art. 1664), unless you have waived them.

voci.d: The client asks me for an extra job, but the price was a lump sum. What do I do?
voci.r: Write the variation with its price and get it approved before you carry it out. The codice civile (Italian Civil Code) requires written proof of the authorisation and, if the price was a lump sum, gives you a right to payment for additions only if it was agreed (art. 1659).

voci.d: When pricing by measurement, who measures at the end?
voci.r: You decide between you, but the safest way is to measure together and sign a sheet with the quantities. Also write the criteria in the quote: how doors and windows are treated, whether waste is included, how skirting board is counted.

voci.d: Can I put lump-sum items and measured items in the same quote?
voci.r: Yes, and it's often the best choice: lump sum for the part you can measure beforehand, by measurement for the part you only find out about while working, like demolition and making good. Just write clearly which rule applies to each item.

voci.d: Is the electrician's per-point quote a lump sum or by measurement?
voci.r: It's in effect by measurement: there's a price for each point and the total follows the number of points installed. If the client wants a fixed total, you can give it as a lump sum and keep the per-point price for additions.

meta.titolo: IVA in a quote for home work
meta.descrizione: IVA in a quote for home work: 10% on maintenance and renovation, working out the beni significativi (significant goods), 22%, new-build homes and inversione contabile (reverse charge).

iva-preventivo-lavori-casa.riga: When the 10% applies, how to work out the beni significativi (significant goods), when you need 22% and when the client applies the IVA.
iva-preventivo-lavori-casa.h1: IVA in a quote for home work: 10%, 22% and beni significativi (significant goods)
iva-preventivo-lavori-casa.intro: Getting the rate wrong in a quote costs you either way. If you put 22% where 10% applied, the customer finds a cheaper competitor just because he did his sums right. If you put 10% where 22% applied, you pay the difference, with penalties and interest, maybe years later. This guide explains the rules that matter for work on homes: the 10% rate for maintenance and renovation, how to calculate the beni significativi (significant goods) using the Agenzia delle Entrate's example (the Italian tax agency), the cases where 22% is needed, new builds and the inversione contabile (reverse charge) between businesses. It does not cover the customer's tax deductions, which change often and are a different subject.
inBreve: On ordinary and extraordinary maintenance of homes, IVA is 10%, but only when you deal with the end customer.

For boilers, windows and doors, sanitaryware and the other beni significativi (significant goods), the 10% covers the item only up to the value of the rest of the job: anything above that goes at 22%.
Restoration, conservation refurbishment and building renovation go at 10% without the beni significativi calculation.
Between firms in the sector, and for some services on buildings, the customer applies the IVA through the inversione contabile (reverse charge).
The rate depends on the property, the type of work and who buys the materials: always have your accountant confirm it.

sezioni.titolo: The three questions to ask before you write the rate
paragrafi: Almost everything is decided by answering three questions, in this order.

punti.titolo: What kind of property is it?
punti.testo: A home, a shared part of a residential block, an ancillary space like a cellar or garage, or a shop, an office, a warehouse. The maintenance reductions only apply to buildings that are mainly private housing.

punti.titolo: What type of work is it?
punti.testo: Ordinary maintenance, extraordinary maintenance, restoration and conservation refurbishment, building renovation or new build. These are the categories in art. 3 of the testo unico dell'edilizia (the Italian consolidated building act), and each has its own IVA rules.

punti.titolo: Who buys the materials, and who is the customer?
punti.testo: Whether you supply the goods as part of the job, or the customer buys them himself. And whether the customer is the private owner, a condominium, or another firm that has subcontracted the work to you.

sezioni.titolo: The 10% rate on home maintenance
paragrafi: Ordinary and extraordinary maintenance on buildings that are mainly private housing carries IVA at 10% (art. 7, paragraph 1, letter b, of legge 488 del 1999). Ordinary maintenance covers repairing, renewing and replacing finishes and the work needed to keep existing systems running; extraordinary maintenance covers work to renew and replace parts, including structural ones, and to build or add sanitary and technical services, without changing volume or use (art. 3 of the testo unico dell'edilizia).

This includes single homes (cadastral categories A/1 to A/11, excluding A/10 offices) even when they are in a non-residential building, buildings where more than half of the floor area is private housing, their shared parts and their ancillary spaces, such as cellars and garages.

The 10% applies only when you deal with the end customer. The following are left out and go at 22%: professionals' fees (designers, site supervisors), work you do as a subcontractor for another firm, and goods you buy yourself from your supplier. And for maintenance there is another rule that matters a lot in a quote: goods supplied by someone other than the person doing the work, or bought directly by the customer, go at the standard rate. If the customer buys the sanitaryware himself in a shop, he pays 22% on it; you invoice only the fitting at 10%.

sezioni.titolo: Beni significativi (significant goods) and the Agenzia's example
paragrafi: In maintenance work, some goods have a separate rule. These are the ones listed in the decreto ministeriale of 29 December 1999 (the ministerial decree on beni significativi): **lifts and hoists, external and internal windows and doors, boilers, video entryphones, air conditioning and air recirculation equipment, bathroom sanitaryware and taps, security systems**. The list is closed, but the Agenzia delle Entrate includes goods with the same function: a pellet stove that also heats the water for the heating system and the domestic hot water is treated like a boiler, one that heats only the room is not.
For these goods the 10% applies only up to the value of the service, that is, the total value of the work minus the value of the beni significativi. The part above that goes at 22%.

The example in the Agenzia delle Entrate (Italian Revenue Agency) guide on renovations goes like this. A job costs 10,000 in total: 4,000 for labour and 6,000 for sanitaryware and taps. The 10% applies to the labour (4,000) and to goods up to the same value (another 4,000). The remaining 2,000 of goods go at 22%. If instead the beni significativi (significant goods) are worth no more than half of the total, the whole job goes at 10%.

The value of the item is the one agreed between the parties, but it cannot be lower than the price you paid for it; if you make the item yourself, the production cost counts. Your mark-up on the item, therefore, ends up in the service part. Separate parts follow a precise rule: if they have their own functional independence (normally roller shutters, shutters and insect screens compared with the window, and always grilles and bars) they count as part of the service and go at 10%; if they are built into the item, they are part of it.

The invoice must show, besides the service, the beni significativi supplied with their value, and keep the 10% IVA and the 22% IVA separate. It is a good idea to set up the quote the same way: the customer sees straight away where the total comes from.

sezioni.titolo: Restoration, conservation refurbishment and renovation: 10% without the calculation
paragrafi: For the more substantial work, that is restoration and conservation refurbishment and building renovation (letters c and d of art. 3 of the testo unico dell'edilizia), the beni significativi (significant goods) rule does not apply. Services under contracts to carry out this work go at 10%, and according to ANCE (the Italian builders' association) even on properties other than homes.

Supplies of finished goods used for the work are also at 10%, while raw materials and semi-finished products are left out. Here, unlike in maintenance, finished goods get the 10% even if the customer buys them directly.

The line between extraordinary maintenance and renovation is not something you decide by eye: it depends on the building permit and on what is really being done. If the customer has a surveyor handling the paperwork, ask how the work is classified and write it in the quote.

sezioni.titolo: When 22% applies
paragrafi: The standard rate is the rule; the others are exceptions. In home work you meet it in these cases.

punti.testo: A shop, an office, a warehouse, even if they are in the same building as the customer's home: for maintenance, 22% applies.

punti.titolo: The excess part of the beni significativi
punti.testo: When the value of the boiler or the windows and doors is higher than the rest of the job, the difference goes at 22%, as in the example above.

punti.titolo: Goods bought by the customer in maintenance work
punti.testo: The customer pays 22% on them to whoever sells them; you invoice only the fitting at 10%.
Design commissioned under a separate contract, site supervision, work done for another firm: the reduced rates do not pass down to the intermediate steps.

punti.titolo: Non-maintenance services in the same contract
punti.testo: If you put maintenance and other services together in the contract without a separate price, you risk losing the reduced rate on the whole amount. Keep the items separate.

sezioni.titolo: Building a new house
paragrafi: Building a new property is not maintenance, and it has its own rules. For contract work to build a non-luxury home, the rate is 4% if the person having it built qualifies for the prima casa relief (first-home tax relief), and 10% in other cases. Luxury homes, meaning those registered as A/1, A/8 and A/9, are outside these reduced rates.

The customer declares the first-home requirements, but you are the one who writes the rate on the invoice. Before you put 4% in a quote, ask the customer for a written declaration and have your accountant check the case: a mistake here is paid on the whole value of the build.

sezioni.titolo: Inversione contabile (reverse charge) between businesses
paragrafi: In some cases you do not put the IVA on the invoice: the customer applies it, adds it to the invoice and pays the tax. This is the inversione contabile (reverse charge), and in building work it covers two situations (art. 17, paragraph 6, of the decreto IVA, the Italian VAT decree).

The first is **subcontracting in the building sector**: services you provide as a subcontractor to a firm that has taken on the job, when both of you work in the construction sector. According to the Agenzia delle Entrate it does not cover sales of goods with installation, where the installation is incidental to the sale of the item.

The second covers **cleaning, demolition, installation of systems and completion services relating to buildings**, provided to a customer who is VAT-registered (soggetto passivo IVA), even if they don't work in construction and even if there is no subcontract. If the plumber installs the heating system in a company's office, as a rule the invoice goes out without IVA, with a note saying inversione contabile (reverse charge). With a private customer, on the other hand, the inversione contabile doesn't apply: you charge the IVA.

One last note: if you are under the regime forfettario (flat-rate scheme), you don't charge IVA to the customer on the invoice. Say so in the quote too, so the total the customer reads is the one they will pay.

sezioni.titolo: How to write it in the quote
paragrafi: A well-made quote makes the IVA clear even to someone who knows nothing about tax. Put the type of property and the type of work at the top of the document, mark the beni significativi (significant goods) in the items with their value, and under the lines put the taxable amount at 10%, the one at 22% if there is one, the two taxes and the total. If the customer buys the materials, the line becomes labour only and you write that.

PreventivoLampo works out the IVA regime from three answers (whether it is a home, what kind of work it is, who buys the materials) and applies the rule of the beni significativi (significant goods) to the items you have marked as such in your [price list](/funzioni/listino-prezzi). At the moment the system calculates 10%, 22% and the split of the beni significativi; inversione contabile (reverse charge), 4% first home and the flat-rate regime not yet, so in those cases check the total before sending it. Under every quote there is a reminder to check with your accountant, and it is a reminder to take seriously.

domande.titolo: Questions about IVA on work in the home

voci.d: I'm redoing the bathroom of a flat: what IVA do I charge?
voci.r: Usually it is extraordinary maintenance on a home, so 10%. Sanitaryware and taps are beni significativi (significant goods): if their value is higher than the rest of the job, the excess part goes at 22%. If the work is classed as ristrutturazione edilizia (building renovation), you don't need to do the beni significativi calculation.

voci.d: The customer buys the boiler themselves: does that change anything?
voci.r: Yes. In maintenance work, goods bought directly by the customer don't get the 10% rate: they pay the ordinary rate to whoever sells them. You invoice only the installation at 10%.

voci.d: Is the roller shutter I fit with the window a bene significativo (significant good)?
voci.r: It depends. According to the Agenzia delle Entrate (Italian Revenue Agency), separate parts with their own functional independence, which is normally the case for roller shutters and insect screens, count as part of the service and go at 10%. If instead they are structurally built into the window frame, they follow its value.

voci.d: I'm working as a subcontractor for a building firm: do I add IVA?
voci.r: If you both work in the construction sector and yours is a supply of services, as a rule the inversione contabile (reverse charge) applies: you invoice without IVA and the main contractor accounts for it. It doesn't apply to sales of goods with installation.

voci.d: I'm doing maintenance in a shop below the customer's home: 10% or 22%?
voci.r: For maintenance, what counts is the property, and a shop is not a home: 22% applies. If the customer is a business and the work is installing systems or completion work, check whether the inversione contabile (reverse charge) applies.

voci.d: Can I put 4% if the customer is building their first home?
voci.r: For a contract to build a non-luxury home, if the customer meets the prima casa (first home) requirements, the rate is 4%. Get their written declaration and have your accountant check the case before you put it in the quote.

preventivo-cliente-straniero.riga: Language, the version that prevails, IVA and withdrawal when the customer doesn't speak Italian.
preventivo-cliente-straniero.h1: Quoting a foreign customer: language, IVA and withdrawal without surprises
preventivo-cliente-straniero.intro: The German customer who has bought a house by the lake, the Dutch family renovating the farmhouse, the English tenant who has just arrived: it happens that you do a site visit in broken English and then have to send a quote to someone who can't read Italian. The rules don't change because the customer is foreign, but the best way to write them down changes a lot. This guide explains which language to write the quote in, how to handle a document in two languages, what happens with IVA and what to say about withdrawal.
inBreve: Work on a house in Italy is invoiced with Italian IVA, even if the customer lives abroad.
The best quote is in two languages, with Italian always included and a clause saying which version prevails.
An ambiguous translation works against you: in contracts with consumers, when in doubt, the interpretation most favourable to the customer wins.
A foreign private customer has the same withdrawal rights as an Italian customer, and must be informed in a way they can understand.

sezioni.titolo: Which language to write the quote in
paragrafi: The practical rule is just one: the customer must understand what they are signing. A quote they can't read doesn't protect them and doesn't protect you, because at the first argument they will say, with some justification, that they didn't know what they were accepting.

The codice del consumo (Consumer Code) goes in the same direction. Terms offered to the consumer in writing must be drafted clearly and in plain language (art. 35), and the information you give before a contract concluded at the customer's home or at a distance must be clear and understandable (art. 49). The same code also upholds the Italian language: information for consumers must be given at least in Italian (art. 9, aimed mainly at products), and when the information goes through an individual distance communication, such as an email, the customer can ask to receive it in Italian (art. 49, paragraph 7).

Put together, these rules all lead to the same solution: a document where Italian is always there and the customer's language sits next to it. Making only the foreign version leaves you exposed. Making only the Italian one leaves the customer exposed, and so you too.

sezioni.titolo: The two-language quote and the version that prevails
paragrafi: A bilingual quote has two columns or two blocks for each item, or the Italian text followed by the translation. At the end you need a clause saying which version prevails if the two don't match, for example: ‘This quote is drawn up in Italian and English. If the two versions differ, the Italian text prevails.’

Why Italian? Because it is the language you work in, the one in which the quote would be read by an Italian consultant, surveyor or judge, and the one in which the technical terms are written. But the clause is not an absolute shield. In contracts with consumers, when the meaning of a clause is doubtful, the interpretation most favourable to the consumer prevails (art. 35, paragraph 2): if the translation says something different from the original and the customer signed trusting their own language, a wrong translation can become your problem.

So the translation must be faithful, not elegant. Short sentences, one thing per sentence, the same numbers in both versions, no summaries. PreventivoLampo makes the quote in the customer's language, choosing from English, German, French, Spanish and Dutch, with a PDF in two languages where the Italian prevails: you always check the Italian version, and that is the one you approve before it goes out.

sezioni.titolo: How to explain the items to someone who doesn't know Italian building work
paragrafi: Many words in a quote have no exact equivalent in other languages, and some Italian habits don't exist elsewhere. For these items it is better to keep the Italian word and add a short explanation, rather than invent a translation the customer won't recognise.

punti.titolo: A corpo e a misura (lump sum and measured)
punti.testo: Explain in one sentence what it means for them: ‘fixed price for all the work described’ or ‘price per square metre, the total is worked out from the final measurements’. It is the difference that matters most for their pocket.
In many countries the customer buys the materials themselves and pays only for labour, or the other way round. Write line by line what you bring and what they bring.

Exclusions that are obvious to an Italian customer (the bricklayer fills the chases, the surveyor applies for the permit) are not obvious at all to a foreigner. Write them all down, even the ones that seem taken for granted.

Dichiarazione di conformità (declaration of conformity), CILA (notice of works start), SCIA (certified notice of works start): keep the Italian name, because that is what the customer will find on the official documents, and add in brackets what each one is for.

Use metric units even with customers who are used to other measures, and watch the commas and full stops in decimals: 1.250 and 1,250 are not the same figure for everyone. Write dates with the month in words.

sezioni.titolo: IVA: Italian IVA applies
paragrafi: For IVA, work on buildings follows a simple rule: services relating to immovable property are treated as supplied in Italy when the property is in Italy (art. 7-quater of the IVA decree). The Agenzia delle Entrate (Italian Revenue Agency) has confirmed this: for these services, all that matters is where the property is, not where the client lives. A bathroom refitted in the Italian home of a customer who lives abroad is therefore invoiced with Italian IVA.

The rate also follows Italian rules, and it depends on the property and the type of work, not on the customer's nationality. Extraordinary maintenance on a home is charged at 10%, with the same rules on beni significativi ("significant goods", the main materials and fittings) that you would apply to an Italian customer. The cases are explained in the guide on [IVA in quotes for home works](/guide/iva-preventivo-lavori-casa).
If the customer is not a private individual but a foreign company, the steps may change, and it is worth checking with your accountant before you send the quote.

sezioni.titolo: What details to ask a foreign customer for
paragrafi: As well as name, surname and the address of the job, ask for their full home address, with the country, an email they actually read, and a phone number with the international prefix. Also ask whether they have an Italian codice fiscale (tax code): people who own a home in Italy often already have one, and you will need it for the invoice.

There is one more reason to ask straight away. If the customer wants to use a tax deduction on the work, the payment must be made with the special bank transfer, which shows the tax code of the person claiming the deduction and your partita IVA (VAT number). A foreign customer often doesn't know about this: telling them before they pay from their foreign account saves them from losing a benefit, and saves you an unhappy customer once the work is done.

Agree on how they will pay too: a transfer from a foreign bank can arrive with different charges or timings. Write your IBAN and your bank's BIC code in the quote, and state that any bank charges on the transfer are paid by whoever sends it.

sezioni.titolo: The right to withdraw, explained in their language
paragrafi: Under the codice del consumo (Consumer Code), a foreign private customer is a consumer like any other. If the contract is made at their home or at a distance, they normally have 14 days to withdraw (recesso) without giving a reason, and you must inform them before they commit, also handing over the withdrawal form. If the information is missing, the deadline is extended by twelve months.

With a foreign customer the problem is not the rule, it is whether they understand it. Information in Italian handed to someone who can't read it does the bare minimum and leaves the argument open about what they really knew. Better to give it in both languages, like the rest of the quote: with PreventivoLampo, the acceptance page and the withdrawal form are translated into the customer's language.

The deadlines, the exceptions (for example made-to-measure goods or urgent repairs requested by the customer) and what happens if the work starts before the deadline are explained in the guide on [withdrawing from a quote accepted at home](/guide/recesso-preventivo-accettato-a-casa).

sezioni.titolo: The site visit, when you don't understand each other well
paragrafi: The bilingual quote starts from the site visit, and that is where misunderstandings begin. Say the measurements and the choices out loud, show with your hands what you are going to do, and photograph what is to be removed and what is to stay. If the customer sends you messages in their language, reply in writing: a written conversation, even badly translated, is worth more than a spoken one half understood.

The same goes for you. If Italian is not your first language, you can describe the site visit in the language you think best in: PreventivoLampo receives the text, in Romanian, Albanian, Arabic or another language, and the draft quote still comes out in Italian, ready to be translated for the customer.

domande.titolo: Questions about quotes for foreign customers

voci.d: Can I write the quote in English only?
voci.r: You can, but it's not a good idea. The codice del consumo (Consumer Code) requires Italian for information given to consumers, and a document only in English leaves you exposed if a dispute arises in Italy. The most solid solution is a quote in two languages, with a clause saying the Italian version prevails.

voci.d: If the two versions say different things, which one counts?
voci.r: The one named in the clause, usually the Italian. But with a consumer, if the meaning of a clause is doubtful, the interpretation most favourable to them prevails (art. 35 of the codice del consumo). That is why the translation must say exactly the same things as the original.

voci.d: The customer lives abroad: do I charge IVA?
voci.r: Yes, if the property is in Italy. Services relating to buildings are treated as supplied where the property is (art. 7-quater of the IVA decree), regardless of where the customer lives.

voci.d: Is the rate the same as for an Italian customer?
voci.r: Yes. It depends on the type of property, the type of work and who buys the materials, not on the customer's nationality or residence.

voci.d: Does a foreign customer have the right to withdraw?
voci.r: Yes, on the same terms as an Italian customer: if they are a private individual and the contract is made at their home or at a distance, they normally have 14 days. It's best to give the information and the form in their language too.

voci.d: How do I write words that can't be translated, like «a corpo»?
voci.r: Keep the Italian word and add a short explanation in the customer's language, for example «a corpo»: fixed price for all the work described. The customer will find that word on Italian documents and will know what it means.

recesso-preventivo-accettato-a-casa.h1: Withdrawal from a quote accepted at home or online: what tradespeople need to know
recesso-preventivo-accettato-a-casa.intro: A quote signed at the customer's kitchen table is the most common way home jobs begin. Under the codice del consumo (Consumer Code), though, that signature is not the same as one made in a shop: a private customer who signs at home, or accepts at a distance, normally has the right to change their mind within a set time, without giving a reason. If you don't tell them in the right way, that time can last more than a year. This guide explains when the right of withdrawal (recesso) applies, how long it lasts, what you must hand over, what happens if the work starts straight away, and which exceptions matter for tradespeople.
inBreve: The right of withdrawal covers private customers and contracts made away from your premises (for example at the customer's home) or at a distance.

The period is 14 days, 30 if the contract comes from a visit of yours that was not requested. For labour only it starts from signing; if you also supply materials, from the day the customer receives them.
If you don't inform the customer and don't give them the form, the deadline is extended by twelve months.
To start before the deadline runs out, you need an explicit request from the customer, on paper or another durable medium.
Urgent repairs requested by the customer and made-to-measure goods have separate rules.

sezioni.titolo: When the customer can change their mind
paragrafi: The right of withdrawal in the codice del consumo (Consumer Code) applies only to the **consumer**, that is, an individual acting for purposes outside their own business, trade, craft or profession (art. 3). The owner who has their home bathroom redone is a consumer; the company that has its offices redone is not.

And it only applies to two types of contract. The first is the **off-premises contract**: one made with you and the customer physically present together in a place other than your business premises, such as their home (art. 45). A quote signed during the site visit is the typical case. The second is the **distance contract**: one made without you and the customer being physically present together, using only distance communication, within an organised distance sales or services scheme, such as a quote accepted online through the link you sent.

There is a grey area, and it comes up often: the site visit at the customer's home, the quote sent by email the next day, the acceptance by email a week later. How to classify it depends on the circumstances, and the answer is not always clear. The cautious choice, which costs very little, is to act as if the right of withdrawal applied: give the information notice and the form together with the quote.

sezioni.titolo: Work that is excluded
paragrafi: Not all building work is covered. The codice del consumo (Italian Consumer Code) excludes from its rules on distance and off-premises contracts those for **the construction of new buildings and the substantial conversion of existing buildings** (art. 47). The directive these rules come from explains that a substantial conversion is comparable to building a new building, for example when only the façade of an old building is kept.

The same directive makes clear that contracts to build extensions such as a garage or a veranda, and repair and renovation contracts that do not amount to a substantial conversion, stay inside the rules. In plain words: redoing a bathroom, a new electrical system, painting, replacing windows and doors are jobs where, as a rule, the right of withdrawal applies.
Off-premises contracts of very low value are also excluded, below the threshold set by art. 47, unless several contracts made together between the same parties go over it in total.

sezioni.titolo: How long the period lasts
paragrafi: For service contracts the customer has **14 days from the signing of the contract** to withdraw, without having to give a reason (art. 52). The period rises to **30 days** if the contract was made during an unsolicited visit by the professional to the consumer's home. The 30-day rule does not apply to visits the customer asked for: a site visit arranged at their request stays within the 14 days.

Watch out for supply-and-fit quotes. Under the codice del consumo (Italian Consumer Code) a contract covering both goods and work is a sales contract (art. 45), and in a sale the period starts from the day the customer receives the goods (art. 52). Boiler, windows, sanitaryware supplied by you: the period starts when you deliver or fit them, not when the customer signs.

If you don't give the customer the information on withdrawal, the period does not end after 14 days: it ends **twelve months after** the end of the initial period. If you put it right and give them the information within those twelve months, the period ends 14 days after they received it (art. 53). In practice, a quote signed without the information leaves the customer free to withdraw for more than a year, even after the work is finished.
For the customer, what counts is the date they send the notice, not the date you receive it: withdrawal is made in time if it is sent within the period (art. 54).

sezioni.titolo: What you must give the customer
paragrafi: Before the customer commits, the codice del consumo (Consumer Code) requires you to give them, in a clear and understandable way, a series of information: who you are and how to contact you, what the work involves, the total price including taxes, the payment and delivery arrangements and, above all, **the conditions, time limits and procedures for withdrawing, with the standard form** set out in annex I of the code (art. 49). If the right of withdrawal does not apply, you must say so. You can use the standard instructions in the same annex: if you fill them in correctly, your duty to inform on these points is met.

In off-premises contracts the information must be given on paper or, if the customer agrees, on another durable medium, and you must hand over a copy of the signed contract or the confirmation of the contract (art. 50). The code defines a durable medium as any tool that lets you store information and reproduce it unchanged: a PDF sent by email, which the customer keeps and can read again exactly as it was, fits this description.
Remember that, if a dispute arises, **the burden of proving you informed the customer is yours**. A notice read out loud leaves no trace; a form handed over with the quote and a signed copy do.

With PreventivoLampo the customer accepts online through the link, and the acceptance leaves a record of name, date, time and a copy of the accepted PDF; the withdrawal form is also available in the customer's language, if the quote is translated. See [online acceptance](/funzioni/accettazione-online).

sezioni.titolo: If the work has to start before the period ends
paragrafi: It happens a lot: the customer signs on Monday and wants you to start on Wednesday. You can do it, but with one precise step. If the customer wants the service to start during the withdrawal period, you must get **their explicit request on a durable medium**, and have them acknowledge that, once the work has been fully carried out, they will no longer have the right of withdrawal (art. 50).

With that request, if the customer withdraws after the work has started, they owe you an amount proportionate to what you have done up to the moment they told you about the withdrawal, calculated on the total price of the contract; if the total price is excessive, it is calculated on the market value of what you have supplied (art. 57). If, instead, the work has been fully carried out, and it started with the customer's express consent and their acknowledgement that they lose the right of withdrawal, the right no longer exists (art. 59).

Without that request, or if you did not give them the information about withdrawal, a customer who withdraws during the period does not have to pay you anything for the services provided (art. 57). This is the worst case: work done, materials fitted, no right to payment.

That is why it is a good idea to put a separate, clearly visible line in the quote, before signing: «I ask for the work to start before the withdrawal period ends. I know that, if I withdraw after it has started, I will have to pay for what has been done up to that point, and that once the work is complete I can no longer withdraw.» A line the customer signs separately is worth more than any explanation given out loud.

sezioni.titolo: The exceptions: urgent work and made-to-measure goods
paragrafi: The codice del consumo (Consumer Code) rules out withdrawal in some cases that matter closely to tradespeople (art. 59). It is worth knowing them well, because each one has a precise limit.

punti.titolo: Urgent repairs requested by the customer
punti.testo: There is no withdrawal in contracts where the customer expressly asked for your visit for urgent repair or maintenance work: a water leak, a fault in the system. But if during that visit you do extra work or supply goods other than the spare parts needed, the right of withdrawal applies again to that part.

There is no withdrawal for the supply of goods made to measure or clearly personalised, such as windows and doors made to the customer's measurements. When the same contract includes both made-to-measure supply and fitting work, the line between the two parts is not always clear: keep the items separate and, if the amount is significant, ask for advice.

If the contract comes from an unsolicited visit by you to the customer's home, some exceptions, including the one for made-to-measure goods and the one for services already carried out, do not apply. Door-to-door selling is the situation in which the customer is most protected.

For repairs and maintenance expressly requested by the customer and carried out straight away, below a low threshold set by art. 50, the information can be given in a simplified form, with an estimate of the total price before you start.

sezioni.titolo: How the customer withdraws and what happens next
paragrafi: The customer can withdraw with the standard form or with any other explicit statement of their decision: a clear email is enough (art. 54). If you offer them the option of withdrawing by filling in a form on your website, you must confirm to them without delay, on a durable medium, that you have received the withdrawal. For distance contracts made through an online interface, from 19 June 2026 the code also provides for a clearly visible online withdrawal function, with a label such as «withdraw from the contract here», and an acknowledgement of receipt with date and time (art. 54-bis, introduced by decreto legislativo 209 of 2025, i.e. Legislative Decree 209/2025).

After the withdrawal you must refund the payments received within 14 days of being informed. If, however, the work had started at the customer's express request, you can keep or ask for the amount proportionate to what was carried out, as seen above.

Do not confuse this withdrawal with the one in the codice civile (Italian Civil Code). In a works contract (appalto) the client can always withdraw, even after the work has started, but must compensate you for the costs you have incurred, the work carried out and the profit you have lost (art. 1671). The consumer's withdrawal is something else: it applies within a short period, needs no reasons and, if the rules have been followed, does not cover lost profit. To write the rest of the quote, see the guide on [how to write a quote](/guide/come-fare-un-preventivo).

domande.titolo: Questions about withdrawing from a quote

voci.d: The customer signed the quote at their home: can they pull out?
voci.r: If they are a private individual and the job is not a new build or a substantial transformation of the building, as a rule yes: they have 14 days to withdraw without giving reasons, from signing if the quote is for labour only, from the day they receive the materials if you supply them. The period rises to 30 days if the contract comes from a visit of yours that was not requested.

voci.d: What happens if I did not give them the withdrawal form?
voci.r: The period is extended by twelve months after the end of the initial period. If you give them the information late, within those twelve months, the period ends 14 days after they received it. Also, if they withdraw during the period, they owe you nothing for the work already done.

voci.d: Can I start work the day after signing?
voci.r: Yes, if the customer expressly asks you to, on paper or another durable medium, and accepts that once the work is complete they lose the right to withdraw. If they then withdraw after the work has started, they owe you an amount in proportion to what you have done.

voci.d: Does an urgent repair that the customer called me out for carry the right to withdraw?
voci.r: No, if the customer asked you to come for an urgent repair. The right to withdraw does come back for extra work, or for goods other than the spare parts needed, that you offer during the same visit.

voci.d: Can made-to-measure windows and doors be returned?
voci.r: Supplying goods made to the customer's measurements is excluded from the right to withdraw. But if the contract comes from a visit of yours that they did not ask for, this exception does not apply. And when the contract also includes fitting work, it is best to keep the items separate.

voci.d: Does the right to withdraw also apply to business customers?
voci.r: No. The right to withdraw in the codice del consumo (Italian Consumer Code) only covers consumers, that is, individuals acting for purposes outside their trade or profession. With a business, the rules of the codice civile (Civil Code) apply, including the client's right to withdraw under art. 1671.

voci.d: Does a quote accepted online follow different rules?
voci.r: It is usually a distance contract, with the same 14-day period. For contracts made through an online interface from 19 June 2026, the codice del consumo (Consumer Code) also requires a clearly visible function to withdraw online, with confirmation of receipt.
